nameStory: The "bitternut" name comes from its nuts, which are so bitter that even squirrels often leave them alone! It's also called "yellowbud hickory" for its distinctive bright yellow winter buds that stand out like little beacons against the gray bark. Some folks call it "swamp hickory" because it tolerates wetter soils better than most of its hickory cousins.
description: Bitternut hickory is a large deciduous tree that can grow 50-75 feet tall with a straight trunk and oval crown. It's one of New England's most widespread hickories, recognizable by its smooth gray bark and compound leaves made up of 7-9 leaflets arranged feather-like along a central stem. Like all hickories, it produces hard-shelled nuts, though these are too bitter for most creatures to enjoy. This tough tree can live up to 200 years, making it a long-term resident of New England's forests.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Bright sulfur-yellow winter buds that practically glow against the bark - no other tree in New England has buds quite this color. They're somewhat flattened and lack scales, feeling smooth to the touch.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-9 lance-shaped leaflets arranged feather-style along a central stem. The leaflets feel smooth and thin compared to other hickories, turning golden-yellow in fall.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Relatively smooth gray bark with shallow furrows, much less shaggy than shagbark hickory. Run your hand along it - it feels fairly smooth with gentle ridges rather than peeling plates.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Round to egg-shaped nuts enclosed in thin husks that split only halfway down when ripe, revealing extremely bitter nuts that taste awful if you're brave enough to try one.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall tree with a straight trunk and oval crown, often growing in moist areas where other hickories struggle. Branches tend to be more slender than other hickory species.

habitat: Look for bitternut hickory in moist, rich soils along stream valleys, floodplains, and lower slopes throughout New England. It's more tolerant of wet conditions than most hickories, so you'll often find it mixed with maples, ashes, and elms in bottomland forests. It also grows on well-drained upland sites but really thrives where there's consistent moisture.

seasonality.spring: Leaves emerge later than many trees, and small yellowish-green catkin flowers appear in May. The famous yellow buds are still visible early in the season before leaf-out.
seasonality.summer: Full canopy of compound leaves provides dense shade, and developing nuts begin forming in their green husks.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn a beautiful golden-yellow color, and nuts ripen and fall. The bitter nuts often remain on the ground since few animals eat them.
seasonality.winter: The brilliant sulfur-yellow buds are at their most obvious and diagnostic, standing out dramatically against bare gray bark and snow.

funFact: Bitternut hickory produces nuts so intensely bitter that they contain natural compounds that can actually make your mouth go numb - it's nature's way of saying 'don't eat me!' Even desperate squirrels in harsh winters will often pass them by for almost anything else.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other hickories, but those bright yellow winter buds are a dead giveaway - no other hickory has them. In summer, remember that bitternut typically has more leaflets (7-9) than shagbark hickory (usually 5), and its bark stays much smoother.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the shortest-lived hickory, 200 years is still an incredibly long lifespan by human standards! Bitternut hickory is also the northernmost member of the 'pecan hickories,' a group that includes the familiar pecan tree of the South.
compareHints: Among New England hickories, bitternut is the easiest to identify thanks to its unique yellow buds. Shagbark hickory has distinctive peeling bark and usually 5 leaflets, while pignut and mockernut have brown buds and different bark patterns. If you see yellow buds on a hickory, you've found your bitternut!

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's hickories, shagbark is the only one with bark that peels in long, dramatic strips - other hickories have tight, furrowed bark.
Pignut hickory has much smoother bark than the dramatically peeling shagbark hickory, and smaller, less noticeable buds than the large, fuzzy-budded mockernut hickory.

Among New England hickories, mockernut is the only one with consistently fuzzy leaf undersides - shagbark hickory has peeling bark plates, bitternut has bright yellow buds, and pignut has smooth leaves and smaller nuts.

Red hickory differs from shagbark hickory by having smooth bark instead of distinctive shaggy plates, and from pignut hickory by typically having 5 leaflets instead of 7, plus sweeter nuts and reddish inner bark.
Among New England hickories, shellbark stands out for its larger nuts and more dramatic bark peeling compared to shagbark hickory.
